The Blacktip jumprock (Moxostoma cervinum) is a relatively small-bodied catostomid endemic to the upper Roanoke and Chowan River drainages of Virginia and North Carolina. Field surveys of adult specimens from these systems indicate that individuals attain a maximum total length of 19 centimers [Li = 19 centimers], a value that places this species among the smaller members of the genus Moxostoma. Examinations of museum collections and recent seine-haul data suggest that the wet weight of newly hatched yolk-sac larvae, immediately following eclosion from the demersal egg, is approximately 0.0019 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0019 grams]. This extremely low mass at the alevin stage reflects the modest size of the fertilised ovum, which typically measures around 1.54 millimeters in diameter. The resulting lecithotrophic larva depends entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves during the first several days after emergence from the chorion, before commencing first exogenous feeding and the transition to an actively growing pelagic larva.

Gonadal development and the onset of sexual maturation in Moxostoma cervinum have been assessed through histological examination of preserved specimens collected across multiple seasons. The total length at which 50 percent of individuals display active gametogenesis, interpreted as the attainment of puberty, is 11 centimers [Lp = 11 centimers]. This size threshold corresponds to a standard length of approximately 9.33 centimers and aligns with a body condition typical of fish transitioning from the juvenile stage to reproductive competence. Using the length–weight relationship derived for this species, where mass scales as 0.00490 times total length raised to the power of 3.10, the wet weight at puberty can be estimated at 8.3 grams [Wwp = 8.3 grams]. This value suggests that individuals commit to reproductive activation only after accumulating a substantial somatic mass, reflecting a life-history strategy that prioritises early growth and predator avoidance before allocating resources toward vitellogenesis and spermiation.

Reproductive output in Blacktip jumprock has been inferred from studies of the closely related greater jumprock, Moxostoma valenciennesi, which shares a similar spawning ecology. During a single spawning event in early spring, gravid females release a substantial clutch of adhesive, demersal eggs. Field observations of nest sites at a water temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C] indicate that individual females produce approximately 15,441 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 15,441 eggs per spawning event], and typically complete one such event per year [F_R_i = one such event per year]. This annual reproductive schedule is synchronised with the thermal regime of the Roanoke drainage, where cold winter temperatures delay gonadal recrudescence until late winter, and the 14 °C thermal optimum appears to maximise embryonic survival and hatching success in the incubating egg.

Adult body size in Moxostoma cervinum exhibits limited variation across its restricted geographic range, with most populations converging on a similar asymptotic mass. Using the length–weight conversion established from a large sample of sexually mature adults, the ultimate wet weight of fully grown individuals attains 45.1 grams [Wwi = 45.1 grams]. This value corresponds to the 19 centimeter maximum total length and represents a typical endpoint of somatic growth for the species. The body plan at this size is characterised by a streamlined, subcylindrical form with a ventral sucker mouth adapted for benthic feeding on insect larvae and organic detritus. Comparative data from congeneric species such as Moxostoma carinatum and Moxostoma duquesnei indicate that the blacktip jumprock achieves a substantially smaller adult mass, a difference that likely reflects its confinement to high-gradient, cool-water headwater streams where productivity and available growing season are limited.

Longevity in Moxostoma cervinum has been estimated from otolith annuli counts obtained from a multi-year mark-recapture study in the Pigg River system. The maximum recorded lifespan for individuals maintained under natural stream conditions approximates 2,500 days [am = 2,500 days], which corresponds to roughly 6.8 years at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This value was derived from fish captured and aged at a mean annual water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], a thermal regime characteristic of the species' preferred montane habitat. The observed lifespan is intermediate among eastern North American catostomids; for example, Moxostoma erythrurum rarely exceeds 5 years in Virginia streams, whereas the larger Moxostoma macrolepidotum can live beyond 10 years. The relatively modest longevity of the blacktip jumprock, coupled with its early maturation and high fecundity, suggests a life-history strategy that favours rapid population turnover in an environment where stochastic flooding events can cause substantial juvenile mortality.
